analysis.one_liner: Slows meatpacking line speeds, restricts point-based attendance discipline, and adds OSHA protections for meat and poultry workers.
analysis.headline: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill with 7 cosponsors (6 Democrats, 1 Independent) in February 2023, and it never received a committee markup or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required meat and poultry plants to prove worker safety before getting any line-speed waiver, barred federal funding for any policy that speeds up slaughter lines, and restricted no-fault attendance systems that dock workers points — including for legally protected leave like sick time. It would have added $60 million a year for OSHA inspectors, set new safety standards for ergonomics and infectious disease, strengthened protections against retaliation (including threats to report a worker's immigration status), and created a private right of action letting workers sue over unsafe conditions. It also would have restored country-of-origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy, and directed $100 million in grants to smaller processors that sign labor peace agreements with unions.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry processing workers, whom the bill's own findings describe as suffering about twice the amputation rate of the average private-industry worker and musculoskeletal injuries that can exceed 50 percent at some facilities. The bill also would have helped livestock ranchers and dairy producers through country-of-origin labeling, and smaller regional processors through expanded grants.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Agriculture Secretary from issuing line-speed waivers unless safety officials certify the faster pace would not hurt worker safety, after an ergonomic analysis of every affected job [S3].
Prohibits using federal funds for any policy that increases line speeds at meat and poultry plants during the covered period [S3].

Makes it unlawful for any employer with 15 or more employees to run a point-based no-fault attendance policy that penalizes legally protected leave, with a private right to sue for back pay and attorney's fees [S3].
Appropriates $60 million per year from fiscal 2024 through 2029 to hire additional OSHA inspectors [S3].

Requires OSHA standards for ergonomics, prompt medical referrals after injuries, and protection from infectious-disease exposure, plus a permanent regional inspection program covering amputation hazards, bathroom-break access, and chemical exposures [S3].

Expands retaliation protections, including treating a threat to report a worker's immigration status as retaliation, and lets meat and poultry workers sue for compensatory and punitive damages over OSHA violations [S3].
Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork and adds dairy products [S3].

Adds $100 million through fiscal 2032 for meat and poultry processing grants, available only to facilities with labor peace agreements, and bars grant recipients for 10 years from selling to a packer with more than 10 percent market share [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing companies, which would face slower line speeds, more inspections and reporting, restrictions on attendance discipline, new standards for ergonomics and disease control, a private right of action with punitive damages, and country-of-origin labeling costs. Some of those costs could show up in meat prices for consumers.

drawbacks.text: The attendance-policy rules would apply to nearly every employer with 15 or more workers nationwide, not just meatpacking plants, a broad new mandate on general business [S3].

The bill requires a COVID-19 emergency temporary standard within 7 days of enactment while waiving the Regulatory Flexibility Act, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and executive-order cost-benefit review for that rule — skipping the usual analysis of a regulation's costs and effects on small businesses [S3].

New compliance obligations for processors — ergonomic and infectious-disease standards, weekly pandemic reporting, expanded inspections, and country-of-origin labeling — carry real costs for an industry with thin margins, and some of those costs could be passed to consumers in meat prices [S2].
Tight rulemaking deadlines, such as a final ergonomics standard within 30 months, could strain OSHA's capacity even with the added inspector funding [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strong: the bill's findings document that meat and poultry workers suffer about double the amputation rate of average private-industry workers and musculoskeletal injuries that can exceed half the workforce, and that higher line speeds are a recognized injury risk [S3]. The main costs fall on processing companies, and the most aggressive provisions — the economy-wide attendance mandate and the 7-day emergency standard issued without normal cost-benefit review — were the provisions an honest supporter would have expected to be negotiated. On balance the bill targeted one of the most dangerous jobs in the country, and its costs were concentrated on the companies responsible for the conditions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never held a markup or reported it, and it died without a vote when Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Protecting America's Meatpacking Workers Act of 2023 in the Senate on February 2, 2023 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day, and no further action was taken on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored the bill: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the committee taking up the bill or the Senate holding any vote on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meat and poultry processing companies are better off: no slower line speeds, no new OSHA ergonomics or infectious-disease standards, no restrictions on point-based attendance systems, no country-of-origin labeling mandate, and no new limits on spot-market purchases or sales to dominant packers took effect.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on February 2, 2023

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in February 2023 and never held a markup or reported it to the Senate during the Congress

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: Long opposed line-speed limits, mandatory country-of-origin labeling, and stricter OSHA enforcement in meat and poultry plants, and no member of the Senate majority moved the bill

sides.party_line_note: All eight Senate sponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and no roll-call votes ever occurred because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to speed up slaughter lines without safety certification, subjected them to more inspections, new ergonomics and disease standards, restrictions on attendance discipline, and worker lawsuits with punitive damages. Their interest in keeping current speeds and enforcement levels ran against the workers' interest in safety.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers with dominant market share
industries.note: The bill would have restored country-of-origin labeling, limited spot-market livestock purchases by packers, and barred grant-funded facilities from selling to any packer with more than 10 percent market share for 10 years — measures aimed at reducing the largest packers' market power.

The bill would have added $100 million through fiscal 2032 for processing grants and $500 million for local agriculture markets, with grants conditioned on labor peace agreements — directing federal money toward smaller plants and unionized workforces.

Restored country-of-origin labeling would have let beef, pork, and dairy carry labels identifying where the animals were raised, which producer groups have long sought to distinguish domestic product from imports.
